name: Kalimpong
tagline: The wool-trade town between Deolo and Durpin hills
meta_description: Kalimpong on a budget: Bhutanese past, Tibetan wool trade, Dr Graham's Homes, monasteries, nurseries, shared jeeps, homestays and real 2025–26 costs.
summary: Kalimpong is a market town at 1,247 m on a saddle between Deolo and Durpin hills, about 70 km from Siliguri. Once Bhutanese and later the hub of the Tibetan wool trade, it is cheaper and calmer than Darjeeling, with monasteries, nurseries, a twice-weekly haat and good local food.

local_story.title: Bhutan's outpost, then the wool market of Tibet
paras: Kalimpong changed hands more than most hill towns. It was part of the Sikkimese world, and is said to have come under Bhutan in 1706; the Bhutanese built Thongsa Gompa here in 1692, still the town's oldest monastery. After the Anglo-Bhutan war of 1864–65, the Treaty of Sinchula handed Bhutan's land east of the Teesta to the British, and in 1866 Kalimpong joined Darjeeling district. Explanations of the name differ: the most quoted is Tibetan for the stockade or assembly of the king's ministers, but there is also a Lepcha reading, 'hillock of assemblage', and a story about the kaulim plant.

Scottish missionaries arrived in the 1870s, when the Rev. William Macfarlane opened the first schools. In 1900 the Rev. Dr John Anderson Graham started the St Andrew's Colonial Homes for Anglo-Indian children with six children in one cottage; it is now Dr Graham's Homes, spread over the slopes of Deolo. At the same time the town became India's main market for Tibetan wool. Mule caravans came down from Lhasa and Gyantse over Jelep La and through Pedong, and traders' families settled around the bazaar.

The 1962 war closed Jelep La and the trade collapsed almost overnight. The town reinvented itself with schools, nurseries and tourism, and the Tibetans who came after 1959 rebuilt their monasteries here. Tagore spent summers at Gauripur House between 1938 and 1940, and his poem Janmadin was broadcast from Kalimpong in 1938. Kalimpong became the headquarters of its own district in February 2017.

did_you_know: The 13th Dalai Lama stayed in Kalimpong in 1910 while in exile, decades before the 14th Dalai Lama consecrated Zang Dhok Palri on Durpin hill in 1976.
Kalimpong cheese and the hand-rolled milk 'Kalimpong lollipops' began at the Swiss Welfare Dairy of Father André Butty, a Swiss Jesuit refused entry to Tibet in the 1950s. The dairy closed in 1990.
Around 300 species of orchid grow around Kalimpong, and the town's nurseries have exported orchids, gladioli and cacti for decades.
intro: Kalimpong is the working town of the eastern Darjeeling hills: smaller than Darjeeling, a bit lower and warmer at 1,247 m, and much cheaper. It sits on a saddle with Deolo hill (1,704 m) to the north and Durpin hill (1,372 m) to the south, and the bazaar fills the dip between them. You come here for monasteries, old mission schools, plant nurseries, the twice-weekly haat, and for Kanchenjunga at dawn from the two hilltops.

It is also the natural base for the villages east of the Teesta: Lava, Rishyap, Kolakham and Neora Valley up the road, Pedong and Sillery Gaon on the old trade route, Lolegaon and Charkhole further on. Shared jeeps to most of them leave from the Motor Stand in the morning. Two nights in town and two or three in a village is the trip we suggest most often.
facts: Monasteries, wool-trade history, nurseries, cheese and lollipops
Jio, Airtel and BSNL good in town
costs: Reserved car from NJP or Bagdogra
Momos and tea in the bazaar

highlights.title: Zang Dhok Palri on Durpin
highlights.text: Founded in 1957 by Dudjom Rinpoche and consecrated by the 14th Dalai Lama in 1976, this monastery on Durpin hill keeps the 108 volumes of the Kangyur. Go at 7 am for prayers, then walk the ridge past the golf course to Morgan House.

highlights.title: The Wednesday and Saturday haat
highlights.text: Twice a week the haat bazaar near the Motor Stand fills with farmers from the villages: squash shoots, ferns, dried fish, churpi, bamboo baskets and Bhutanese chillies. Go before 10 am, when the best produce is still on the ground sheets.

highlights.title: Dr Graham's Homes
highlights.text: Founded in 1900 with six children in one cottage, the school now spreads over the slopes of Deolo, with stone cottages, a chapel and a farm. Visitors may walk the main road through the campus during the day; respect the school's rules.

highlights.title: Thongsa Gompa
highlights.text: Kalimpong's oldest monastery, built by the Bhutanese in 1692, when the town belonged to Bhutan. It is small and easy to miss in the bazaar, which is part of its charm. Look for the row of prayer wheels along the wall.

highlights.title: Orchid and cactus nurseries
highlights.text: Kalimpong grows orchids, gladioli and cacti for sale across India. Pine View Nursery is known for its cactus collection, and family nurseries below town grow orchids that flower mainly from March to May. Small entry fees apply at some.

highlights.title: Kanchenjunga from two hills
highlights.text: Deolo, at 1,704 m, and Durpin, at 1,372 m, give the best dawn views in town. On clear mornings from October to April, Kanchenjunga rises to the north-west above the hills of Sikkim, well over 80 km away as the crow flies.

how_to_reach.text: Shared jeeps leave Siliguri for Kalimpong from the stands near the SNT bus terminus and Panitanki More when full, ₹200–300 a seat, 3–3.5 hours via NH10, Sevoke and Teesta Bazar. NH10 has had repeated landslide and flood closures since October 2023; when it is shut, vehicles divert via the Dooars and Gorubathan or via Darjeeling and Peshok. Check current status before you travel.

A reserved car from NJP railway station or Bagdogra airport costs about ₹3,500–5,000 and takes 3–3.5 hours when NH10 is clear, longer on diversions. Book through your hotel or take one from the prepaid stands. Ask the driver which road is open before you leave.

NBSTC and private buses run from Siliguri's Tenzing Norgay bus terminus to Kalimpong several times a day, cheaper than jeeps at around ₹150–200, but slower. They suit travellers with light bags and time to spare.

Shared jeeps run from Darjeeling (about 50 km, 2.5–3 h, ₹200–250) via Peshok and Teesta Bazar, and from Gangtok (about 75 km, 3 h, ₹250–350) via Rangpo and Melli. Both use stretches of NH10 along the Teesta, so check current status before you travel.

where_to_stay: Kalimpong has three useful stay zones. The bazaar and Main Road around the Motor Stand have budget hotels at ₹1,200–2,500 a room, handy for early jeeps but noisy. Durpin hill is quiet and green, with West Bengal Tourism's Morgan House and the smaller Tashiding Tourist Lodge in the same estate. Below town on the Siliguri side, Holumba Haven puts you inside an orchid nursery. The forest corporation's Sailabash lodge sits in the forest compound, and Deolo Tourist Lodge is on top of Deolo hill for sunrise. For village homestays, base yourself in Sillery Gaon, Icchey Gaon or Ramdhura instead.
tips: Plan your town day around Wednesday or Saturday, when the haat bazaar is on.
Shared jeeps to Lava, Pedong and Lolegaon leave in the morning, so do village transfers before noon.
Buy Kalimpong cheese and lollipops from small dairies and shops in the bazaar, and ask who made them, as the original Swiss Welfare Dairy closed in 1990.
Avoid driving up from Siliguri on the Durga Puja and Diwali weekends, when NH10 traffic and fares are at their worst.
NH10 closures since October 2023 can add hours to the trip: ask your hotel about the road the day before and check current status before you travel.

experiences.title: Morning prayers at Zang Dhok Palri on Durpin
experiences.summary: Climb Durpin hill early for prayers at Zang Dhok Palri, the monastery consecrated by the 14th Dalai Lama in 1976, then walk the quiet ridge past the army golf course to the lawns of Morgan House.
body: Zang Dhok Palri Phodang stands on top of Durpin hill, 1,372 m, about 4 km from the bazaar. Dudjom Rinpoche, one of the great Tibetan lamas who came south after 1959, established it in 1957, and the 14th Dalai Lama consecrated it in 1976. Its name refers to Guru Rinpoche's palace on the Copper-Coloured Mountain, and the building is designed to echo it. Inside are the 108 volumes of the Kangyur and texts carried out of Tibet.

Come by 7 am, when the monks chant and the light is low across the valley. Walk clockwise around the building, spin the prayer wheels with your right hand, and keep your voice down in the prayer hall. Photography rules differ room by room, so ask. The upstairs galleries have wall paintings worth looking at closely.

Afterwards, walk down the ridge road: the army golf course spreads across the hilltop, and Morgan House, the 1930s mansion now run by West Bengal Tourism, is about 15 minutes away. On clear mornings between October and April you will see Kanchenjunga to the north-west. A taxi from the bazaar costs about ₹200–300 one way; the walk back to town takes 45 minutes.

faqs.q: What time does Zang Dhok Palri open?
faqs.a: The monastery usually opens to visitors from early morning until late afternoon, roughly 7 am to 5 pm, with a lunch break in some seasons. Morning prayers around 7 am are the best time. Hours change on festival days and during special rituals, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee at Durpin monastery?
faqs.a: No, entry is free. A small donation in the box is welcome. Some rooms may ask you not to photograph, so look for signs or ask a monk. Remove shoes where asked, dress modestly, and walk clockwise around the building and its prayer wheels.

faqs.q: How do I get to Durpin hill from Kalimpong?
faqs.a: A taxi from the Motor Stand costs about ₹200–300 one way and takes 15 minutes. On foot it is about 4 km uphill, around an hour. Many people take a taxi up for prayers and walk back down past Morgan House and the golf course.

experiences.title: Haat day, Kalimpong cheese and lollipops
experiences.summary: Walk the twice-weekly haat with the villagers who come in to sell, then hunt down Kalimpong's own cheese and the milk lollipops first made by a Swiss Jesuit's dairy. Breakfast of momos and sha phaley on the way.
body: On Wednesdays and Saturdays the haat bazaar near the Motor Stand fills with farmers from the villages around Kalimpong. Spread out on sheets you will find squash shoots, ningro ferns, red cherry pepper, dried fish, hard churpi, bamboo baskets, brooms and seasonal fruit: oranges in winter, plums in early summer. Go early, before 10 am, when the best produce has not yet gone.

Kalimpong's cheese and lollipops have a story. In the 1950s Father André Butty, a Swiss Jesuit hoping to go to Tibet, was stopped near Kalimpong and stayed. He set up the Swiss Welfare Dairy to help a mission orphanage, making a firm Gouda-style cheese and hand-rolled lollipops of milk boiled down in iron pans. The dairy closed in 1990, when his visa was not renewed, but local makers still produce both.

Ask in the bazaar's grocery shops for Kalimpong cheese, and for lollipops by the piece. Then sit down for breakfast: steamed momos at ₹60–120 a plate, sha phaley (Tibetan meat pies) or a bowl of thukpa. Leave space for a cup of local tea.

faqs.q: Which days is the Kalimpong haat bazaar?
faqs.a: The main haat is held on Wednesdays and Saturdays near the Motor Stand, when villagers bring produce and crafts into town. Shops in the bazaar open daily. Arrive by 9 am for the fullest market. Days can shift around festivals, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Where can I buy Kalimpong cheese?
faqs.a: Look in grocery and dairy shops around the bazaar and Main Road, and ask for local Kalimpong cheese. Supplies are small and vary by season. The original Swiss Welfare Dairy closed in 1990, so today's cheese comes from smaller local makers. Keep it cool if you are carrying it home.

faqs.q: What are Kalimpong lollipops?
faqs.a: They are hand-rolled sweets made from milk boiled down to a dark, chewy toffee, wrapped around a stick. They were first made at Father André Butty's Swiss Welfare Dairy in the mid-20th century. Local makers still sell them by the piece or in packets in the bazaar, for a few rupees each.

experiences.title: Orchid and cactus nurseries of Kalimpong
experiences.summary: Kalimpong has grown and sold plants for generations: around 300 orchid species grow in these hills, and the town's nurseries ship orchids, gladioli and cacti across India. Visit two or three for a gentle half day.
body: Kalimpong's mild climate, at about 1,250 m, suits plants that would sulk in Darjeeling's cold. Around 300 species of orchid grow in the hills around the town, and families here have been growing and selling plants for decades: orchids, gladioli bulbs, amaryllis and, more surprisingly, cacti and succulents. Nurseries are spread around the town, some on the main roads and some down lanes.

Pine View Nursery is known for its cactus collection, rows of greenhouses full of spines from the other side of the world, a strange sight in a monsoon town. Family nurseries below town, such as the one around Holumba Haven guesthouse, grow orchids that flower mainly from March to May, with some species in autumn. Ask before you walk into private greenhouses, and do not touch the plants.

Combine nurseries with a quiet walk: many sit on the lower roads towards Siliguri or on the Rinkingpong side. A half-day taxi costs about ₹1,500–2,000. If you buy plants, ask about carrying them home; orchids travel badly in hot trains and some cannot be taken on flights.

faqs.q: When do orchids flower in Kalimpong?
faqs.a: Most orchids flower between March and May, with a smaller show in October and November. Nurseries have something in bloom much of the year, because they grow many species. For wild orchids on trees, look in the forests around Lava and Lolegaon in spring.

faqs.q: Is Pine View Nursery worth visiting?
faqs.a: Yes, if you like plants. It is known for a large cactus collection in greenhouses, unusual for a rainy hill town. Allow about an hour. There is usually a small entry fee. Opening hours vary with the season, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I buy orchids in Kalimpong and take them home?
faqs.a: You can buy plants and bulbs, and nurseries often pack them for travel. Orchids do not like heat, so long, hot train journeys can harm them. Ask the nursery about airline rules and plant care. Carrying plants abroad usually needs phytosanitary papers, so ask before buying.

experiences.title: Dr Graham's Homes and the Deolo slope
experiences.summary: Walk through the campus of Dr Graham's Homes, founded in 1900 with six children in a single cottage, then climb on to the top of Deolo hill for the view. A slow half day of stone cottages, pine and Scottish mission history.
body: In 1900 the Rev. Dr John Anderson Graham, a Scottish missionary already working in Kalimpong, opened the St Andrew's Colonial Homes for Anglo-Indian children who had nowhere to go. It began with six children in a single cottage. The idea was a village of cottages, each with its own house-parents, rather than a large orphanage, and that is still how the campus looks today: stone cottages named after their donors, spread across the lower slopes of Deolo.

The school is still working, so you visit as a guest. The main road through the campus is generally open to walkers in daylight. Look for the chapel, the cottages and the old farm buildings. Do not enter buildings or photograph children without permission, and check at the gate if you are unsure.

From the school, continue uphill to the Deolo park on top of the hill, at 1,704 m, about 2 km further. There is a small entry fee, lawns, paragliding take-offs and, on clear mornings, Kanchenjunga to the north. Take a taxi back to town for about ₹200–300, or walk down in 45 minutes.

faqs.q: Can tourists visit Dr Graham's Homes?
faqs.a: Visitors can usually walk the main road through the campus in daylight and look at the chapel and cottages from outside. It is a working school, so do not enter buildings, disturb classes or photograph children without permission. Rules can change during exams or events, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Who founded Dr Graham's Homes?
faqs.a: The Rev. Dr John Anderson Graham, a Scottish missionary in Kalimpong, founded it in 1900 as the St Andrew's Colonial Homes for Anglo-Indian children. It started with six children in one cottage and grew into a campus of cottages on the slopes of Deolo hill. It was later renamed after him.

faqs.q: How far is Deolo hill from Dr Graham's Homes?
faqs.a: Deolo park on top of the hill is about 2 km above the school by road, a 30–40 minute uphill walk or a 10-minute taxi ride. The top is at 1,704 m, the highest point around Kalimpong, with lawns, a small entry fee and Kanchenjunga views on clear mornings.

faqs.q: Is Kalimpong worth visiting?
faqs.a: Yes, especially if you want a hill town that is cheaper and calmer than Darjeeling. Kalimpong has real history, from Bhutanese rule to the Tibetan wool trade and Scottish missions, good monasteries, a twice-weekly haat, nurseries and Kanchenjunga views from Deolo and Durpin. It is also the best base for Lava, Pedong, Sillery Gaon and Lolegaon.

faqs.q: How many days are enough for Kalimpong?
faqs.a: Two nights cover the town: one day for Durpin, Morgan House and the monasteries, one for Deolo, Dr Graham's Homes, the nurseries and the haat if it falls on a Wednesday or Saturday. Add two or three nights in a village such as Lava, Sillery Gaon or Icchey Gaon for a full trip.

faqs.q: Is Kalimpong better than Darjeeling?
faqs.a: They are different. Darjeeling has the toy train, tea estates and Tiger Hill; Kalimpong is smaller, warmer, cheaper and less crowded, with more village escapes nearby. Many travellers do both, two nights each, linked by a 2.5–3 hour jeep ride via Peshok and Teesta Bazar.

faqs.q: Is NH10 open to Kalimpong now?
faqs.a: NH10 between Sevoke and Rangpo has had frequent closures since the October 2023 Teesta flood, including a major landslide near Coronation Bridge in June 2026. When it is shut, vehicles use diversions through the Dooars and Gorubathan or via Darjeeling. Ask your hotel the day before and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How much does a Kalimpong trip cost per day?
faqs.a: On a shoestring, about ₹1,500–2,200 per person per day, with shared jeeps, a budget hotel or homestay and bazaar food. A comfortable trip with a reserved car and a heritage room at Morgan House runs about ₹4,000–6,000 per person per day. The biggest cost is usually the reserved car.

faqs.q: Can I see Kanchenjunga from Kalimpong?
faqs.a: Yes, on clear days, mostly from October to April. The best spots are Deolo hill, at 1,704 m, and Durpin hill near Zang Dhok Palri. Go at dawn: clouds usually build by mid-morning. In the monsoon, from June to September, views are rare.

faqs.q: Is Kalimpong good for a family trip?
faqs.a: Yes. Drives within the town are short, Deolo park has lawns and pony rides, and the nurseries, monasteries and Science Centre suit children. Stay at a WBTDC lodge or a family hotel with heaters in winter. Avoid long same-day transfers to Lava or Lolegaon after lunch with small children.

faqs.q: What is Kalimpong famous for?
faqs.a: Kalimpong is known for its history as the Indian market of the Tibetan wool trade until 1962, for Dr Graham's Homes, founded in 1900, for Zang Dhok Palri monastery on Durpin, for its orchid and cactus nurseries, and for Kalimpong cheese and lollipops first made by a Swiss Jesuit's dairy.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for Kalimpong?
faqs.a: No permit is needed for Kalimpong town or the surrounding villages for Indian or foreign visitors. You need entry permits for Neora Valley National Park, arranged at Lava. If you continue into Sikkim, foreign nationals need a Restricted Area Permit. Rules change, so check current status before you travel.
